name: LifeWire Chroma Subdermal Display System
body_location: subdermal full-body or partial (arms, face, torso — user-specified at installation)
description:
The Chroma system is a network of bioluminescent micro-emitter filaments implanted just beneath the epidermis, suspended in a biocompatible gel matrix that bonds with the body's existing fascia. The filaments are individually addressable via a wireless protocol paired to a companion app or neural tap, allowing the user to push color patterns, animated designs, gradients, and reactive displays across the skin's surface in real time. The system draws power from the body's ambient thermal differential and requires no external charging. Color depth spans the full visible spectrum with optional ultraviolet expression for users who purchase the UV-Extend firmware package. Pattern libraries are sold as subscription content or one-time purchases through the LifeWire marketplace.

Chroma is the defining cosmetic implant of the working and middle tiers — as normalized as hair dye was in the twentieth century, but infinitely more expressive. the Gray Zone kids save for months to get a partial install on their forearms; Tier 3 professionals run subtle animated gradients under their collars for job interviews or social events. Parents get matching family patterns for holidays. Couples synchronize their displays. Artists use their own skin as portfolio. The implant has collapsed the tattoo industry as it existed and spawned an entirely new creative economy around pattern design, with independent artists selling skin-display content through third-party marketplaces. Most users update their look weekly; some change it hourly.
installation_requirements: Outpatient clinic or licensed LifeWire installation kiosk; partial installs (single limb) take under two hours; full-body installs require a day clinic visit
maintenance: Annual gel matrix refresh at any LifeWire service kiosk; firmware updates pushed wirelessly; no battery replacement required

cultural_context: Chroma is so thoroughly normalized in GLMZ that walking into a Tier 2 neighborhood without any skin display is often read as a deliberate aesthetic statement — the 'blank' look, sometimes called going 'matte,' has its own subculture among minimalists and certain religious communities. On the Gray Zone, Chroma patterns function as social signifiers, neighborhood markers, and gang-adjacent symbols — the corponations have tried to trademark certain pattern families without much success. In the Spire, raw Chroma is considered slightly gauche; the ultra-wealthy prefer bespoke bioweave from Helix or custom dermal installations that don't use the LifeWire marketplace. The implant has generated significant legal controversy around workplace expression rights, with several landmark rulings establishing that employers cannot mandate employees suppress their Chroma displays during off-hours.

story_hooks: A Chroma pattern appearing spontaneously on a user's skin — one they never loaded — turns out to be a steganographic message embedded in a corrupted firmware update, and someone very dangerous sent it
A black-market pattern file is circulating in the Gray Zone that causes Chroma displays to broadcast a forbidden political symbol; users don't know it's in their library until enforcement shows up
A Tier 5 fashion house is quietly buying up independent Chroma pattern artists under coercive contracts, and one of those artists wants out
